questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095109/assets/f531f2467284ef84e0af0758a8e8554f1e5f72ea08d30d0b80c83076fbe5d7a3.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,0)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(0+t(1-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & =1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095109/assets/f402fe97e6f76cd94b94331e7f30ddb09c978c93b86ce112a5232042a2f741cc.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2y\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-12{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to Y
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095109/assets/b21c9c11aa3320a729db0d8a71f5c89069d46527e78dfc76b47ae3925387c770.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3x+2y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-2,2)$ to the point $(-1,1),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨t-2,\,2-t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-2,2)$ and $(-1,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-2+t(-1-(-2))),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨t-2,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3x+2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(t-2)+2(2-t) \\  & =3t-6+4-2t \\  & =t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2)\cdot (-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095109/assets/be3ad044a611d99e67c89d053d4878a2835be65828a4dc9300697bfd61822994.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the below-left quarter of the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(-1,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{u}^{3}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{u}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-[(0)^{4}-(-1)^{4}] \\  & =-(-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095109/assets/f83043b44a8ad9181e66de57357397deb49c4b0e79b5e6e16330305a58391148.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(4,0)$ to the point $(-4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
